rationale: Unsupported system components asks two questions in sequence: what components are in use, and are any of them past vendor support. The first is answered exactly by a repository — the lockfile pins every direct and transitive dependency to a version, syft resolves the same tree into an SBOM, and the Dockerfile names the base image tag the container is built from, all at a commit and all anchored — and that inventory is normally the part an assessment has to take on trust from a spreadsheet. The advisory collectors add a weaker signal on top: a component still receiving fixes is one the vendor still supports.

remainder.control: Support status itself. Whether a named version is still supported by its developer or vendor comes from a lifecycle source outside the repository — an end-of-life feed, a registry deprecation flag, a support contract — and collectors here do not reach the network. Replacement, the control's actual requirement, is an act rather than an artifact: the repository can show an unsupported component is still pinned, never that a plan exists to replace it.
remainder.boundary: And the repository set. The lockfile and SBOM are an inventory of the components of one checkout, which is the strongest form this control's evidence takes and still not the system inventory the control asks about: components deployed from other repositories, or vendored outside the manifest, are absent from the evidence in exactly the way a supported component is absent — indistinguishable without the human-named repository set.

citesUpstream.note: Both planes rate SA-22 partial and both name the decision half as the remainder — that an unsupported component is replaced, or its continued use justified and approved, is a human record. The routes differ in what they treat as the population. Upstream's is detection: a scanner identifies components past end of support, and their rationale grants that the scanned population is narrower than the control's, since firmware, appliances and managed-service versions never appear in a manifest. Ours is the inventory itself — the lockfile and SBOM are the component list an assessment normally takes on trust, committed and anchored — so the two are complementary rather than redundant: theirs answers which components are stale, ours answers what the component set IS and that nobody edited it. Their scanning platform raises SA-09 and CA-03 by their own account; the cost of ours declining the network is that support status stays in the remainder, which is the trade stated plainly rather than hidden.

externalSystem: Nothing — which is the sharp end of the difference on this control. Determining supported versions is what pulls a component-inventory tool onto a vendor's API, and that API is an external system. rampscan declines the network and therefore declines the lifecycle feed too: the remainder above is the price of the external system this plane does not add.
